item.title: NISQ Preparation of Conditional Thermal States for Precision Thermometry
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Variational preparation of conditional thermal states on trapped ions yielded estimated sub-quantum Fisher information ℐest∗=2.00 for a two-qubit transverse-field Ising model at target inverse temperature βtgt=0.51 (theoretical sub-QFI ℐ∗(βcal)=3.01, relative error 33.6%). The corresponding two-qubit Gibbs state preparation circuit was too noisy to estimate sub-QFI.

Grade 0.385 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Computing in the NISQ era and beyond” · Emery Doucet, Reece Robertson, Nicholas Donatelli, Shou-I Tang, Sebastian Deffner, Akira Sone

Figure

Finite-difference ratio 8r(β,β′) versus calibrated inverse temperature β′ for two-qubit transverse-field Ising states around βtgt=0.51. Hardware experiments on the conditional thermal state reproduce the theoretical sub-quantum Fisher information curve away from the β′→β divergence, while Gibbs state data are dominated by gate noise.

Asks

Can conditional thermal states be prepared variationally on near-term trapped-ion processors and benchmarked via direct sub-quantum Fisher information measurement to demonstrate their thermometric advantage?

But

Device hardware noise reduced the experimental CTS sub-QFI estimate below the theoretical Gibbs value; hardware errors prevented meaningful sub-QFI extraction for the two-qubit Gibbs state.

Tools

IonQ Forte Enterprise 1 trapped-ion computer · Variational quantum algorithm based on free energy minimization · Constant-depth swap-free circuit for sub-quantum Fisher information estimation

Abstract

The ability to prepare thermal states on gate-based quantum computers is an important building block for quantum computation, both with regard to the implementation of certain classes of quantum algorithms as well as to the study of quantum thermodynamics in and out of equilibrium. A useful generalization of the standard notion of a thermal state which appears naturally in the study of quantum work distributions is the conditional thermal state, which is conditioned on the use of an accessible pointer basis associated with a measurement apparatus. Among other uses, it has been proven that conditional thermal states can outperform ordinary thermal states in quantum thermometry. In this work we demonstrate the preparation of conditional thermal states of few-qubit systems implemented on IonQ's cloud-based quantum computers across a range of temperatures. To validate their performance advantage in thermometry, we measure the sub-quantum Fisher information (a lower bound on the quantum Fisher information) of the prepared states, which can be computed via a constant-depth quantum circuit without tomography.

item.title: Unitary Synthesis with a Unary Tracker
item.description:
Worth a look new method — T-count O(K+NL) for synthesizing an n-qubit unitary with N=2n, L=n+log⁡(1/ϵ), and K mixing branches, using N+O(L) clean ancillas. Space-depth volume is O(N2) using n≤a≤N ancillas at circuit depth O(N2/a).

Grade 0.379 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Fred Sun

Asks

Can the cosine-sine decomposition reach near-O(2n) scale T-count by making classical Boolean lookups free in T-gates?

Before

Synthesizing branches independently yields naive T-count O(N2L) (where L=n+log⁡(1/ϵ)).

But

Requires classical specification of U, unrestricted connectivity, and access to an ideal phase-gradient catalytic state. Mixing branch count K is factorization-dependent and can reach Θ(N2) in worst case.

Tools

unary tracking register · cosine-sine decomposition (CSD) · quantum Shannon decomposition (QSD) · phase-gradient catalytic state · Fredkin gates

Abstract

This manuscript studies general unitary synthesis using unary-encoded ancillary register. Our first construction focuses on the T-cost of unitary synthesis. We maintain a unary register that coherently tracks the computational-basis label of the data. This allows Boolean lookups to use only CNOTs and shares the precision-dependent synthesis cost across the branches of each cosine-sine decomposition (CSD) factor. For a classically specified n-qubit unitary with K mixing branches in its CSD, we obtain T-count O(K+NL) using N+O(L) clean ancillas, where N=2ⁿ and L=n+log(1/ε). We also give a related construction that directly applies the unitary onto a unary register to implement disjoint branches in parallel. Combining this with the quantum Shannon decomposition gives space-depth volume O(N²) using arbitrary single-qubit gates and CNOTs, which matches the asymptotically optimal bound.

item.title: Quditology: harnessing many levels for quantum information processing
item.description:
Worth a look review — Survey of qudit quantum information hardware demonstrates that multi-level d>2 architectures match the Hilbert space of 70 qubits using 24 qudits with d=8, achieving gate-depth reductions exceeding one order of magnitude in dedicated quantum simulations.

Grade 0.369 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Computing in the NISQ era and beyond” · Abhijit Chakraborty, Zheng Shi, Noah Goss, Irfan Siddiqi, Barry C. Sanders, Christine A. Muschik

Figure

Landscape of qudit implementations showing controllable qudit dimension d on the horizontal axis versus the number of interacting qudits n on the vertical axis across experimental platforms.

Asks

What is the current experimental state of the art in high-fidelity state preparation, control, measurement, and fault tolerance across diverse qudit platforms?

But

Increased spectral crowding, heightened sensitivity to phase decoherence, energy relaxation across higher levels, and elevated classical and quantum crosstalk.

Tools

trapped ions · superconducting circuits · solid-state nuclear spins · photonic circuits · neutral atoms

Abstract

Quantum computing offers the prospect of surpassing classical computation on certain tasks by leveraging quantum coherence and entanglement. However, a significant gap remains between current quantum hardware and the requirements to transcend what classical computers can achieve, with decoherence limiting the capacity of storing quantum information and the number of logical steps that can be executed reliably. In the long term, fault tolerance bridges this gap, but simply changing the numerical base from binary to higher base d is a viable way to 'squeeze more juice'---get more quantum information processing---from a quantum computer of given size. Additionally, for quantum simulations, qudits offer a natural encoding scheme for high-dimensional physical degrees of freedom. Here, we review recent experimental progress in high-fidelity preparation, control, and measurement of qudits across various platforms such as trapped ions, superconducting circuits, solid-state nuclear spins, photonic systems, and neutral atoms. We highlight early demonstrations of qudit-based quantum simulation, computation and error suppression enabled by these developments, heralding the transition of qudits from conceptual constructs to viable building blocks for quantum technologies. Finally, we outline key challenges and potential future directions for scalable qudit quantum information processing.

item.title: Estimating the Trotter error via phase analysis
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Trotter operator-distance error approximates as τ2‖Φˆ2‖ for small step size τ, where ‖Φˆ2‖=12‖∑p1∑p2<p1[Hˆp1,Hˆp2]‖. This expression upper bounds the error per step at large step counts s due to destructive interference across steps.

Grade 0.365 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Maxime Dion, Benjamin D'Anjou

Figure

Rescaled Trotter error η versus dimensionless step size ‖Hˆ‖τ across multiple random Hamiltonians. Exact error tracks close to η=0 (the proposed phase operator estimate ‖Φˆ2‖τ2) rather than the standard upper bound η=1.

Asks

Why are general operator-distance Trotter error bounds excessively loose in practice, and how can the actual error be estimated more tightly?

Before

Childs et al. (2021) general operator-norm bound prefactor α1=12∑p1‖∑p2<p1[Hˆp1,Hˆp2]‖, which applies the triangle inequality over outer sums and overestimates error for Hamiltonians with more than two noncommuting terms.

But

Small Trotter step size τ regime; finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces; unperturbed unitary evolution without physical noise.

Tools

Hermitian phase operator formalism · BCH / Magnus-type expansion in nested commutators · Adjoint representation sinc filtering

Abstract

Good Trotter error estimates are crucial to correctly assess the resources required to perform an approximate time evolution with a target accuracy. General bounds for finite-size quantum systems are found to be very loose in practice, and it is therefore highly desirable to improve on them. In this work, we analyze the Trotter error in terms of the spectrum of a phase operator that we construct from the Hamiltonian. In the limit of a small Trotter step size, we obtain an estimate of the Trotter error written in terms of a sum of nested commutators between terms of the Hamiltonian. The structure of this estimate allows us to naturally explain the looseness of general bounds. We show that even for a finite step size, our estimate typically remains more accurate than general bounds. Moreover, we argue that it becomes an upper bound for the Trotter error per step in the limit of a large number of steps, reflecting the destructive interference of the errors across steps. Our results provide useful practical heuristics for resource optimization in quantum simulations.
